cases.n: IICSA — Anglican Church investigation report
cases.place: England and Wales (Church of England, Church in Wales)
cases.who: Church of England; Church in Wales
cases.cover: Inquiry found the Church gave 'excessive attention' to alleged perpetrators over victims, ignored safeguarding advice, and used forgiveness to justify failing to respond to allegations.
cases.d: The Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse published its Anglican Church investigation report on 6 October 2020. It counted 390 convicted offenders associated with the Church of England from the 1940s to 2018 and warned the true scale cannot be known. In 2018 alone, dioceses received 2,504 safeguarding concerns, 449 of them about recent child sexual abuse. It found deference to authority, clericalism and taboos about sexuality kept victims from disclosing, and that bishops kept safeguarding decision-making power.
cases.cite: IICSA, The Anglican Church: Safeguarding in the Church of England and the Church in Wales, 6 October 2020; Church Times, 9 October 2020

cases.n: Diocese of Chichester — clergy abuse (IICSA case study)
cases.who: Church of England, Diocese of Chichester
cases.cover: Clergy with known concerns (Rideout, Cotton, Graves, House) were given or kept permission to officiate; Cotton's prior conviction for indecent exposure involving a child sat in his diocesan file but was not shared with police; an archdeacon declined to report a serious indecent assault; Sussex Police dropped a 1997–98 investigation and later destroyed its records.
cases.d: IICSA found the Diocese of Chichester had more child sexual abuse convictions than any other Church of England diocese. Roy Cotton had been ordained in the 1960s despite a prior conviction involving a child. Sussex Police investigated Cotton and Colin Pritchard in 1997–98 without charges; when Northamptonshire Police revived the case in 2006, Sussex Police had destroyed its records. The diocese's 2008–09 Past Cases Review missed the scale of abuse, and real action against abusers began only with Operation Perry in 2011.
cases.cite: IICSA, Anglican Church Case Studies: Chichester/Peter Ball, conclusions

cases.n: Bishop Peter Ball — conviction and Church collusion
cases.victims_note: 18 young men at sentencing (2015); IICSA describes 17 teenagers and young men, 1977–1992
cases.who: Church of England; 'Give a Year to God' scheme
cases.cover: Lambeth Palace received seven letters supporting complainant Neil Todd's allegations in 1992 but passed only the least incriminating one to police; Archbishop George Carey wrote to the Gloucestershire Chief Constable; Ball's twin brother, also a bishop, phoned potential complainants to dissuade them; Ball accepted a caution in 1992 and was soon returned to ministry, including work in schools.
cases.d: Peter Ball, former Bishop of Lewes and of Gloucester, ran a 'Give a Year to God' scheme for young men that the Church did not monitor. Gloucestershire police investigated in 1992 and he accepted a caution for one offence; IICSA found the Crown Prosecution Service advice to caution was wrong and other charges were possible. He pleaded guilty in 2015 and on 7 October 2015 was jailed for 32 months for offences against 18 young men over 15 years. Dame Moira Gibb's review 'An Abuse of Faith' (June 2017) found the Church colluded with Ball; Lord Carey stepped back from ministry. IICSA also noted the Duchy of Cornwall bought a property rented to Ball and his brother.
cases.cite: IICSA Chichester/Peter Ball conclusions; Gibb, An Abuse of Faith (GS Misc 1172), June 2017; sentencing coverage 7 October 2015

cases.n: John Smyth — Iwerne camps, Zimbabwe and South Africa (Makin Review)
cases.place: Iwerne camps (Dorset) and Winchester College; later Zambesi Ministries camps, Zimbabwe; Cape Town
cases.victims_note: Makin Review: between 115 and 130 boys and young men; at least 85 of them in Zimbabwe and South Africa (Church Times, citing the review)
cases.who: Iwerne Trust (evangelical camps), Church of England; Zambesi Ministries (Zimbabwe); Anglican Church of Southern Africa
cases.cover: A 1982 internal Iwerne Trust report (the Ruston Report) described the beatings; the Makin Review found an 'active cover-up' by its recipients; police were not told until 2013. The review called Smyth 'a problem solved and exported to Africa' and found no evidence of proactive attempts to alert Zimbabwean authorities.
cases.d: John Smyth QC, chair of the Iwerne Trust 1974–81, beat and abused boys and young men he met through the evangelical Iwerne camps and Winchester College's Christian Forum. After the 1982 Ruston Report he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, founding Zambesi Ministries camps for boys in 1986; a 16-year-old died at one of his camps in December 1992 and Smyth was arrested in 1997 but never charged anywhere. Refused re-entry to Zimbabwe, he moved to South Africa in 2001 and the review found abuse likely continued until his death in Cape Town on 11 August 2018. Keith Makin's review was published on 7 November 2024; Archbishop Justin Welby resigned on 12 November 2024.
cases.cite: Makin, Independent Learning Lessons Review: John Smyth QC (Church of England), published 7 November 2024; Church Times, 15 November 2024

cases.n: Royal Commission data — Anglican Church of Australia
cases.victims_note: 1,082 complainants about 1,115 alleged incidents reported 1980–2015; some incidents dated back to 1950
cases.who: Anglican Church of Australia
cases.d: Data released at the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse in March 2017 showed 1,082 people lodged complaints of child sexual abuse about 1,115 incidents in the Anglican Church of Australia between 1980 and 2015. The complaints identified 569 alleged perpetrators who were clergy, teachers or volunteers, plus 133 whose church roles were unknown (702 in total).
cases.cite: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, Case Study 52 data, March 2017; Gulf News/AP

cases.n: Canada residential schools run by Anglican, United and Presbyterian churches
cases.victims_note: About 37,000 of roughly 80,000 Common Experience Payment applicants also claimed sexual abuse, serious physical abuse or other wrongful acts (all churches combined); about 180,000 First Nations, Inuit and Métis children attended over 150 years
cases.who: Anglican Church of Canada (ran over 30 schools), United Church, Presbyterian Church, with the Catholic Church and federal government
cases.cover: The schools were a federal government system run by churches.
cases.d: Canada's Indian residential schools were run for the federal government by the Anglican, Catholic, Presbyterian and United churches; the Anglican Church of Canada operated more than 30. In April 2013 Truth and Reconciliation Commission chair Justice Murray Sinclair said about 37,000 former students had filed claims for sexual abuse, serious physical abuse or other wrongful acts, and asked the public to imagine 'a school where half of the students suffered sexual and physical abuse'. The TRC's final report followed in 2015.
cases.cite: Anglican Journal, 25 April 2013 (TRC Quebec National Event)

cases.n: Southern Baptist Convention — 'Abuse of Faith' investigation
cases.place: Southern Baptist churches nationwide (most convicted offenders in Texas)
cases.who: Southern Baptist Convention churches
cases.d: The Houston Chronicle and San Antonio Express-News published 'Abuse of Faith' on 10–11 February 2019. They found about 380 Southern Baptist ministers and volunteers had faced allegations of sexual misconduct over the previous 20 years, with more than 700 victims. Many pleaded guilty or were convicted, more from Texas than any other state.
cases.cite: Houston Chronicle / San Antonio Express-News, 'Abuse of Faith', February 2019; Baptist Standard, 11 February 2019

cases.n: Southern Baptist Convention — Guidepost report and secret list of accused ministers
cases.victims_note: The list released on 26 May 2022 had 703 entries of accused ministers, mostly 2000–2019
cases.who: Southern Baptist Convention Executive Committee
cases.cover: Former Executive Committee officials D. August Boto and Roger Oldham kept a private list of abusive ministers, but no one acted to keep them out of SBC pulpits; survivors met 'resistance, stonewalling, and even outright hostility' and were told church autonomy prevented action; a few senior leaders and outside counsel focused on avoiding liability.
cases.d: Guidepost Solutions, hired after SBC delegates demanded an outside probe in 2021, released its report on 22 May 2022. It found a few senior Executive Committee leaders had for about two decades controlled the response to abuse reports to limit legal liability, ignoring or disbelieving survivors. The Executive Committee then published the previously secret list, 205 pages and 703 entries, on 26 May 2022.
cases.cite: Guidepost Solutions report, 22 May 2022; AP (Spokesman-Review), 23 May 2022; WSOC-TV/AP, 27 May 2022

cases.n: Frank Houston — Royal Commission Case Study 18 (Assemblies of God / Hillsong)
cases.who: Assemblies of God in Australia (now Australian Christian Churches); Hillsong Church
cases.cover: When allegations surfaced in 1999, Brian Houston, then National President of the Assemblies of God and Frank Houston's son, confronted his father, who confessed; Brian Houston and the National Executive did not refer the matter to police.
cases.d: Pastor Frank Houston sexually abused a young boy in the 1970s. The Royal Commission's Case Study 18 findings (November 2015) found that Brian Houston and the national executive did not report the allegations to police when they emerged in 1999, and that Brian Houston had a conflict of interest as both national president and the son of the alleged perpetrator. Frank Houston died in 2004 without being charged.
cases.cite: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, Case Study 18 findings, November 2015

cases.n: Brian Houston acquitted of concealing father's abuse
cases.who: Hillsong Church
cases.d: Hillsong founder Brian Houston was charged with concealing a serious indictable offence of another person, namely his father Frank Houston's abuse of a boy in the 1970s, which court papers said he knew of by 1999. On 17 August 2023 Magistrate Gareth Christofi found him not guilty, ruling he had a reasonable excuse for not reporting.
cases.cite: Religion News Service, 16–17 August 2023

cases.n: ForuM study — German Protestant Church (EKD)
cases.place: EKD, Hanover (all regional churches and Diakonie)
cases.victims_note: 2,225 documented victims in files reviewed; researchers estimated up to 9,355 minors
cases.who: Evangelische Kirche in Deutschland (EKD) and Diakonie
cases.cover: Researchers said regional churches delivered documents slowly despite a contract, so the study could not be completed; co-author Martin Wazlawik called the figures 'the tip of the tip of the iceberg'.
cases.d: The ForuM study, commissioned by the EKD in 2020 and led by Hanover University of Applied Sciences and Arts, was released on 25 January 2024. Files reviewed showed 2,225 victims and 1,259 potential perpetrators among ministers, employees and volunteers since 1946, with a projected estimate of up to 9,355 abused minors. EKD head Kirsten Fehrs called it a 'massive failure' toward victims.
cases.cite: ForuM research network, 25 January 2024; AFP (Citizen Digital), 25 January 2024

cases.n: Jehovah's Witnesses — Royal Commission Case Study 29
cases.who: Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Australia (Jehovah's Witnesses)
cases.cover: None of the 1,006 alleged perpetrators recorded since 1950 was reported to police by the church. The 'two-witness rule' required two witnesses before elders' judicial committees could act, blocking 125 allegations; 401 members were expelled after internal hearings and 230 later readmitted.
cases.d: At hearings in July–August 2015, the Royal Commission was told the Watch Tower Society's files held 1,006 alleged perpetrators of child sexual abuse since 1950, including 579 confessions, and that none had been reported to secular authorities. The Commission referred 514 alleged perpetrators to police. Its November 2016 report found the organisation did not respond adequately to child sexual abuse and that its two-witness rule showed a serious lack of understanding of abuse.
cases.cite: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, Case Study 29 report, November 2016; AFP (News24), 27 July 2015

cases.n: Conti v. Watchtower — Fremont congregation, California
cases.who: Watchtower Bible and Tract Society (Jehovah's Witnesses)
cases.d: In June 2012 an Alameda County jury found the Watchtower Society liable for abuse of a girl by a congregation member and awarded punitive damages, later reduced. In April 2015 the California appeals court reversed punitive damages but upheld $2.8 million in compensatory damages; the case settled during further appeal. Other US civil cases followed, including a $13.5 million San Diego judgment in 2014 (vacated 2016, settled 2018) and a $35 million Montana verdict in 2018 reversed in 2020.
cases.cite: Doe (Conti) v. Watchtower, California Court of Appeal, April 2015 (summarised in Wikipedia with citations)

cases.n: Warren Jeffs — FLDS child 'marriages' conviction
cases.place: Yearning For Zion ranch, Eldorado, Texas; Short Creek (Colorado City AZ / Hildale UT)
cases.victims_note: Texas conviction concerned girls aged 12 and 15
cases.who: Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints (FLDS)
cases.d: FLDS president Warren Jeffs was added to the FBI Ten Most Wanted list on 6 May 2006 and arrested in Nevada on 28 August 2006. A 2007 Utah conviction for accomplice to rape was reversed in 2010, and Arizona charges were dismissed in 2010. In August 2011 a Texas jury convicted him of two counts of sexual assault of a child, girls aged 12 and 15 he had taken as 'spiritual wives', and he was sentenced to life plus 20 years. Texas authorities had raided the YFZ ranch on 7 April 2008 and taken custody of about 416 children, who were later returned after courts found the removal unjustified.
cases.cite: AP, 4–9 August 2011; Wikipedia 'Warren Jeffs' (index)

cases.n: Bountiful, B.C. — parents convicted of taking 13-year-old to marry Warren Jeffs
cases.who: FLDS, Bountiful community
cases.d: In February 2017 a B.C. Supreme Court judge in Cranbrook convicted Brandon James Blackmore and Emily Gail Blackmore of removing a child from Canada for sexual purposes: in 2004 they took their 13-year-old daughter to the Utah–Arizona line to be married to Warren Jeffs, then 48. Both were jailed in August 2017. In the same trial James Oler was acquitted of a related charge.
cases.cite: Salt Lake Tribune, 7 February 2017; AP, 11 August 2017

cases.n: James Oler — removing a 15-year-old from Canada to marry
cases.who: FLDS, Bountiful community
cases.d: Former FLDS Bountiful bishop James Oler was first acquitted in 2017; the B.C. Court of Appeal ordered a new trial. In May 2019 he was found guilty of removing a child from Canada, having taken a 15-year-old girl to the United States in 2004 to be married to an older FLDS member. On 29 August 2019 he was sentenced to 12 months in jail and 18 months' probation. Separately, Oler (5 wives) and Winston Blackmore (24 wives, 1990–2014) were convicted of polygamy in July 2017.
cases.cite: CBC News, 29 August 2019; RNZ/AFP, 25 July 2017

cases.n: Malka Leifer — Adass Israel School, Melbourne
cases.victims_note: Warrant listed at least eight pupils; convicted over abuse of two sisters
cases.who: Adass Israel School (ultra-Orthodox community school)
cases.cover: In March 2008, after a teacher confronted her, the school arranged and paid for a 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel for Leifer and four of her children without telling police. In Israel, then deputy health minister Yaakov Litzman pressured ministry staff to alter psychiatric evaluations so she would appear unfit for extradition; her lawyers sought more than 70 hearings and appeals.
cases.d: Headmistress Malka Leifer abused pupils at Melbourne's ultra-Orthodox Adass Israel School between about 2003 and 2007. The school flew her to Israel in March 2008. Australia issued a warrant in 2014 for 74 offences involving at least eight pupils; she was arrested in Israel in August 2014, found in 2019 to have faked mental illness, and extradited on 25 January 2021. On 3 April 2023 a Melbourne jury found her guilty of 18 charges including rape, and in August 2023 she was sentenced to 15 years. In 2015 the Supreme Court of Victoria had ordered the school and Leifer to pay a former pupil about AU$1.27 million.
cases.cite: County Court of Victoria verdict 3 April 2023 (Al Jazeera); Wikipedia 'Malka Leifer affair' (index)

cases.n: Yaakov Litzman — breach of trust for shielding Malka Leifer
cases.who: Israeli Ministry of Health; ultra-Orthodox Agudat Yisrael party
cases.cover: A government minister pressured ministry psychiatrists to alter evaluations of an extradition suspect.
cases.d: Former Israeli health minister Yaakov Litzman signed a plea deal in January 2022 admitting breach of trust for pressuring Health Ministry employees to change psychiatric evaluations so that Malka Leifer would appear unfit to stand extradition trial. He resigned from the Knesset in June 2022 and on 8 August 2022 the Jerusalem Magistrate's Court sentenced him to eight months' probation and a fine of about US$900. Australian Jewish groups condemned the deal as lenient.
cases.cite: AP, 8 August 2022

cases.n: Charity Commission inquiry — Manchester New Moston Jehovah's Witnesses congregation
cases.who: Manchester New Moston Congregation of Jehovah's Witnesses (charity); Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Britain
cases.cover: Trustees dismissed one allegation as a matter between two teenagers, did not enforce restrictions on the accused, and the victims were effectively required to repeat their allegations at an internal hearing in front of the abuser, who was allowed to question them. The charity did not give the Commission accurate and complete answers. The Watch Tower Society fought the inquiry through five courts and tribunals until 2016.
cases.d: Allegations of child abuse against a trustee of the New Moston congregation were made in 2012 and 2013; he was later convicted of two counts of indecent assault. The Charity Commission opened a statutory inquiry on 27 May 2014 and published its report on 26 July 2017, finding the trustees had not adequately dealt with the allegations. The Commission also ran a wider inquiry into the Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Britain.
cases.cite: Charity Commission for England and Wales, Manchester New Moston Congregation of Jehovah's Witnesses inquiry report, 26 July 2017

cases.n: A v Watchtower — High Court damages over Peter Stewart abuse
cases.who: Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Britain
cases.d: On 19 June 2015 the High Court awarded £275,000 damages to a woman abused as a child by Jehovah's Witness ministerial servant Peter Stewart, holding the organisation liable; appeals were refused. In a separate 2014 case in Barry, Wales, elder Mark Sewell was sentenced to 14 years for eight sex offences, and most of the investigating elders declined to give evidence.
cases.cite: A v Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society, High Court, 19 June 2015 (summarised in Wikipedia with citations)

cases.n: Utrecht University / WODC study — Jehovah's Witnesses in the Netherlands
cases.victims_note: 751 people shared experiences through the study's contact point; 27% of cases led to a police report
cases.who: Jehovah's Witnesses (Netherlands)
cases.d: A study by Utrecht University researchers led by Kees van den Bos, commissioned by the Ministry of Justice's research centre WODC, was published on 23 January 2020. 751 participants reported experiences; only 27% of cases led to a police report. Victims were critical of internal handling by elders; the researchers recommended better support, elder training, an internal reporting centre, and that lawmakers consider a duty to report abuse to police.
cases.cite: Utrecht University / WODC, 'Sexual abuse and willingness to report sexual abuse within the Jehovah's Witnesses community', 23 January 2020

cases.n: Pennsylvania grand jury — Jehovah's Witnesses child sexual abuse charges
cases.place: Harrisburg, Pennsylvania (defendants from Philadelphia, Delaware, Butler and Berks counties)
cases.who: Jehovah's Witnesses congregations in Pennsylvania
cases.d: A statewide investigating grand jury in Harrisburg, opened after a county prosecutor's referral, heard dozens of witnesses about abuse in Jehovah's Witness congregations. On 7 July 2023 Attorney General Michelle Henry announced charges against five more men, bringing the total to 14 charged; one earlier suspect killed himself before arrest. One former elder was later convicted in Lancaster County.
cases.cite: AP (WITF), 7 July 2023

cases.n: Latter-day Saints abuse help line — Bisbee, Arizona case (AP investigation)
cases.who: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
cases.cover: After the father confessed to his bishop, the bishop called the church's abuse help line; church lawyers told him the clergy-penitent privilege meant he had to keep it secret. AP reported the abuse continued for about seven years afterwards. The help line, set up in 1995, routes calls that pose legal risk to church attorneys.
cases.d: Paul Douglas Adams, a Border Patrol employee and church member in Bisbee, abused his daughter from age 5 and later a second daughter, and filmed the abuse; he stopped only when arrested in 2017 and died by suicide in jail before trial. An AP investigation published 4 August 2022 found church officials had known for years through confessions. Arizona law, like more than 20 states, lets clergy withhold abuse learned in confession. The church disputed the AP's account.
cases.cite: Associated Press investigation, 4 August 2022

cases.n: Colonia Dignidad — Paul Schäfer convicted of abusing 25 children
cases.place: Colonia Dignidad (now Villa Baviera), near Parral, Maule Region
cases.victims_note: Conviction covered 25 minors abused 1993–1997; 26 children's reports led to the 1996 warrant; the colony held about 100 children at its peak
cases.who: Colonia Dignidad / Sociedad Benefactora y Educacional Dignidad (German sect)
cases.cover: Chile's Rettig Report (1991) found the colony served as a detention and torture centre for Pinochet's secret police (DINA) from 1973; German diplomats 'at best looked away' from the 1960s to the 1980s (German Foreign Minister Steinmeier, 2016). Schäfer fled in 1997 and hid in Argentina for eight years.
cases.d: Former Luftwaffe medic and lay preacher Paul Schäfer, wanted in Germany since 1959 for abusing two boys in Siegburg, founded Colonia Dignidad in Chile in 1961. The colony ran a free school and clinic for local children, some of whom were illegally adopted into the sect. Charged in 1996 with abusing children, Schäfer disappeared on 20 May 1997; he was convicted in absentia in 2004 with 26 other members, found in Tortuguitas near Buenos Aires in March 2005, and on 24 May 2006 sentenced to 20 years for 20 counts of indecent assault and 5 of forced sodomy against 25 minors, plus about US$1.4 million to families. He died in prison in 2010. In January 2013 six former leaders were jailed.
cases.cite: Houston Chronicle/AP, 24 May 2006; MercoPress, 11 March 2005; Wikipedia 'Paul Schäfer' and 'Colonia Dignidad' (index)

cases.n: Germany acknowledges failures over Colonia Dignidad
cases.who: German Foreign Office; Colonia Dignidad
cases.cover: Foreign Minister Frank-Walter Steinmeier said in April 2016 that 'over the course of many years, from the 60s to the 80s, German diplomats at best looked away' and that the embassy failed to shield Germans at the colony.
cases.d: In April 2016 Germany released Foreign Office files from 1986–1996 and the foreign minister admitted diplomats had failed colony residents, including abused children. In 2017 the Bundestag formally acknowledged German responsibility and asked the government to plan an investigation, memorial and help for victims; in 2019 Germany announced compensation payments to victims.
cases.cite: NBC News/Reuters, April 2016; German Foreign Office, 26 April 2016; Deutsche Welle 2018 and BBC 18 May 2019 (via Wikipedia)

cases.n: Re ST (A Minor) — High Court judgment on The Family (Children of God)
cases.who: The Family / Children of God (now The Family International)
cases.d: In a custody case decided on 19 October 1995 after three years of hearings, Lord Justice Alan Ward found that the group, including some top leaders, had in the past sexually abused minors and used severe corporal punishment and sequestration of children. He found these practices had been abandoned by 1995, let the mother keep custody, and required the group to end corporal punishment in the UK and to denounce founder David Berg's writings that had led to children being subjected to sexually inappropriate behaviour. A 2005 group spokesperson acknowledged 'sexually inappropriate advances' in a 1978–1986 transitional period.
cases.cite: Re ST (A Minor), judgment of Lord Justice Ward, 19 October 1995 (summarised by CESNUR, International Journal of Cultic Studies, and Wikipedia)

cases.n: Argentina raids on The Family (Children of God) communes
cases.victims_note: 137 children taken into custody; the judge said 9 showed signs of maltreatment
cases.who: The Family / Children of God
cases.d: On 1 September 1993 Judge Roberto Marquevich ordered raids on Family communes near Buenos Aires; 137 children were taken into state custody and about 30 members arrested. The judge said nine children showed signs of 'cruel and atrocious maltreatment', which the group disputed. Children were later released after examination and no convictions resulted. Raids in Australia (1992, including Panton Hill, Victoria), France and Spain also ended without convictions.
cases.cite: Christianity Today, 25 October 1993; Washington Post/Reuters, 2 September 1993 (via Wikipedia)

cases.n: Twelve Tribes — Bavaria child removals upheld by European Court
cases.place: Klosterzimmern (Deiningen) and a second community, Bavaria
cases.who: Twelve Tribes (Zwölf Stämme)
cases.d: On 5 September 2013 more than 100 Bavarian police removed 40 children from two Twelve Tribes communities after undercover recordings by journalist Wolfram Kuhnigk showed children being beaten with rods; the group says it canes disobedient children. This was physical, not sexual, abuse; the children were placed in foster care. In 2018 the European Court of Human Rights (Wetjen and Others v. Germany) upheld the removals because of the risk of inhuman or degrading treatment.
cases.cite: NPR, 5 September 2013; ECHR, Wetjen and Others v. Germany, 22 March 2018

cases.n: NXIVM — Keith Raniere convicted (including sexual exploitation of a 15-year-old)
cases.who: NXIVM (self-help group run as a cult)
cases.d: A Brooklyn federal jury convicted NXIVM leader Keith Raniere in June 2019 of racketeering, racketeering conspiracy, sex trafficking, attempted sex trafficking, forced labour conspiracy and wire fraud conspiracy. Prosecutors proved as racketeering acts that at 45 he sexually exploited a 15-year-old girl and photographed the abuse. On 27 October 2020 he was sentenced to 120 years and fined $1.75 million.
cases.cite: US Attorney's Office EDNY press release, 27 October 2020

cases.n: Tony Alamo Christian Ministries — leader convicted of transporting girls across state lines
cases.who: Tony Alamo Christian Ministries
cases.d: On 24 July 2009 a federal jury convicted Tony Alamo on all 10 counts of transporting minors across state lines for sex; women testified he had taken them as 'wives' when they were children, some as young as 9. On 13 November 2009 he was sentenced to 175 years and fined $250,000. In 2013 federal authorities moved against 27 properties held by members to collect $2.5 million restitution. He died in custody in 2017.
cases.cite: FBI Little Rock press release, 13 November 2009

cases.n: Agape Boarding School — Christian boys' school, Missouri
cases.who: Agape Boarding School (independent Baptist ministry)
cases.cover: The state Attorney General's office said 22 workers should have been charged with serious crimes, but the county prosecutor charged five with low-level counts; in Missouri only the local prosecutor can file charges.
cases.d: Former students came forward in 2020. In 2021 the school's longtime doctor, David Smock, was charged with child sex crimes and five staff with low-level abuse counts; two later pleaded guilty to misdemeanours. Missouri passed a 2021 law tightening oversight of religious boarding schools. Agape closed on 20 January 2023.
cases.cite: AP (CBS News), 11 January 2023

cases.n: Royal Commission Case Study 22 — Yeshivah Melbourne and Yeshiva Bondi
cases.place: Yeshivah Centre, East St Kilda (Melbourne) and Yeshiva Centre, Bondi (Sydney)
cases.who: Yeshivah Centre / Chabad Institutions of Victoria; Yeshiva Centre – Chabad NSW
cases.cover: The Commission found that the principle of mesirah (not informing on a fellow Jew to secular authorities) as applied in the community discouraged reporting, and survivors who went to police were treated as outcasts. Bondi's Rabbi Yossi Feldman testified he 'was not aware it was illegal to touch a child's genitals'; the Commission found him ignorant of the duty to report.
cases.d: The Royal Commission held hearings in February 2015 on responses to abuse by David Cyprys, David Kramer and Aron Kestecher at Yeshivah Melbourne and Daniel Hayman at Yeshiva Bondi. Its report (released October–November 2016) found 'a marked absence of supportive leadership' for survivors at Yeshivah Melbourne. Its 2017 final report recommended Jewish institutions state that mesirah does not apply to reporting child sexual abuse.
cases.cite: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, Report of Case Study No. 22, 2016

cases.n: Nechemya Weberman — Satmar counsellor, Williamsburg
cases.who: Satmar Hasidic community, Brooklyn
cases.cover: During the case men were arrested for trying to bribe the victim and her husband to drop it; four were later convicted of coercion or witness tampering. Others photographed her on the witness stand and posted the images online.
cases.d: Nechemya Weberman, an unlicensed counsellor in the Satmar community, abused a girl from age 12 to 15. He was convicted on all 59 counts on 10 December 2012 and sentenced on 22 January 2013 to 103 years, later cut on appeal. Brooklyn DA figures showed about 100 of 5,389 sex abuse cases since 2009 came from the Haredi community; critics said DA Charles Hynes's policy of not naming Haredi defendants protected the community.
cases.cite: AP (Times of Israel), 22 January 2013; Wikipedia 'Sexual abuse cases in Brooklyn's Haredi community' (index)

cases.n: AP investigation — sexual abuse in Pakistan's madrassas
cases.place: Pakistan (cases in Kehrore Pakka, Mansehra, Punjab)
cases.victims_note: 359 cases reported in newspapers over 10 years (Sahil tally); a Pakistani official disclosed more than 500 complaints against madrassa teachers in 2004
cases.who: Islamic seminaries (madrassas), over 22,000 registered with at least 2 million pupils
cases.cover: Police are often paid off and refuse to register cases; families of poor victims are pressured to 'forgive' clerics and accept money, which Pakistani law allows; the religious affairs minister dismissed the claims. Police told AP that clerics are almost never convicted.
cases.d: An AP investigation published 21 November 2017 found sexual abuse by clerics was pervasive in Pakistan's madrassas and seldom prosecuted. In one case a 9-year-old's teacher confessed but was freed after the mother 'forgave' him for $300. A follow-up AP investigation in 2020, based on dozens of police reports, found the same pattern.
cases.cite: Associated Press, 21 November 2017; AP/RFE-RL, 14 April 2020

cases.n: Herry Wirawan — Islamic boarding school, Bandung
cases.who: Islamic boarding schools (pesantren) run by the offender
cases.d: Herry Wirawan, head of Islamic boarding schools near Bandung, raped 13 girl students aged 12 to 16 between 2016 and 2021, making eight pregnant. A Bandung court gave him life in prison in February 2022; on prosecutors' appeal the Bandung High Court sentenced him to death on 4 April 2022.
cases.cite: Jakarta Post, 4 April 2022; AP, 5 April 2022

cases.n: Asaram Bapu — convicted of raping a 16-year-old at his ashram
cases.who: Asaram Bapu ashrams
cases.cover: Witnesses in his cases were attacked; a former aide was shot dead in May 2014 and the key witness in the Surat case was shot dead in January 2015.
cases.d: A 16-year-old girl said guru Asaram Bapu assaulted her on 15 August 2013 at his Manai ashram; he was arrested by Jodhpur police on 1 September 2013. On 25 April 2018 a Jodhpur court convicted him of raping a minor and sentenced him to life imprisonment. In January 2023 a Gandhinagar court gave him a second life term in a case brought by two sisters from Surat.
cases.cite: Jodhpur SC/ST court judgment, 25 April 2018 (via Wikipedia 'Asaram' with citations)

cases.n: Nithyananda — Gujarat abduction case and flight from India
cases.who: Nithyananda Dhyanapeetam
cases.d: On 17 November 2019 Gujarat Police registered a case of abduction after a Tamil Nadu couple said three of their children had been taken from Bangalore to Nithyananda's Ahmedabad ashram without consent. Police said on 20 November 2019 that Nithyananda had fled India after skipping hearings, and by January 2020 Interpol had issued a blue corner notice to locate him; he claims to have founded a 'Hindu nation', Kailasa. On 2 February 2024 the Gujarat High Court dismissed the father's habeas corpus petition, finding the daughters were adults who chose to stay with the group. He separately faces a 2010 rape case brought by an adult disciple.
cases.cite: The Hindu, 21 November 2019; NDTV, 22 January 2020; Indian Express, 3 February 2024 (via Wikipedia 'Nithyananda')

cases.n: Manitoba Colony 'ghost rapes' — Mennonite colony, Bolivia
cases.who: Old Colony Mennonite community, Manitoba Colony
cases.cover: The attacks were first blamed on ghosts or demons; a 2013 investigation reported similar assaults continuing.
cases.d: Between 2005 and 2009 men from the Manitoba Mennonite Colony sedated households with an animal anaesthetic spray and raped women and girls, the youngest three years old. In August 2011 a Bolivian court sentenced seven men to 25 years each; a veterinarian from a neighbouring colony who supplied the sedative got 12 years.
cases.cite: TIME, 26 August 2011; BBC News, 16 May 2019 (via Wikipedia 'Manitoba Colony, Bolivia')
